en: Essentials for the Śākya Clan, Volume One.
Compiled by Dharma Master Jù of Tiānxǐ Monastery in Jiānkāng, with the assistance of funds provided by Dharma Master Yuèlún of Yùnlún Mountain in Qiántáng,
who lectured on the Sūtras and Śāstras.
Compiled by the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Shi Daocheng. Daocheng himself, having retired from lecturing at the capital temples and returned to his native village,
first took up residence at Longhua Chan Monastery.
Later, he resided at the Candramaṇḍala Hermitage;
for ten years thereafter, he remained in solitary seclusion,
cutting off all external affairs.
I shall merely read the Tripitaka daily as my regular practice to fulfill my former aspiration.
Nevertheless, when facing the texts while ignorant of their meaning,
I am like a thirsty man drinking from the river.
They are merely able to fill their bellies,
yet they do not know its depth or breadth; or,
when they encounter matters that those who have left the household life ought to know.
I have recorded this at random.
It was in the autumn of the third year of the Tianxi era that His Majesty extended his vast and luminous grace.
I have universally delivered all the novices throughout my realm.
For this reason,
I have collated the texts so that like things follow one another.
Incorporating supplementary materials from various family histories, biographies, letters,
and annotated texts, they were divided into twenty-seven chapters and compiled into three fascicles.
It is titled *The Essential Manual for Buddhists*.
Furthermore, it is intended to provide relief for those who have newly entered the Dharma-gate and know nothing;
should they peruse this compendium...
If one conceals [these matters] within the treasury of the spirit,
one will avoid the reproach of "stealing the robes" for as long as one lives.
This applies even to those of versatile talent and profound learning.
How could one discard the words of the Sage merely because their sincerity is subtle? Such is the intent.
Regarding the titles of the chapters, they are based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which states that Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.
That is to say: knowing all established conventions,
knowing all languages,
and knowing all forms of discourse.
He knows all rules of conduct;
he knows all designations;
he knows all established regulations.
Knowing their conventional designations, knowing their inexhaustibility,
knowing their quiescence, and knowing that all things are empty—
from these [insights], the work is divided into twenty-seven chapters.
Thus, the words and phrases of the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, when examined together, are all subsumed within the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).

Regarding names, titles, residences, ordination, preceptors and disciples, shaving the hair, dharma robes, the rules of the precepts, and midday meals—concerning these names, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: [text follows].
A *xing* (surname) is that which binds and unifies a lineage for a hundred generations so that it is not divided;
a *shi* (clan name) is that which distinguishes the specific lineages from which one's descendants originate.
The Genealogy of the Śākya Clan states:
"The origin of the rise of surnames and given names is fundamentally intended to summon and designate various natures."
Therefore, they are designated according to their respective categories.
There are four castes in India: first, the Kṣatriya, which refers to the lineage of hereditary kings;
second, the Brāhmaṇa—translated in the language of Qin as "Outer Intent"—which refers to the lineage whose pure conduct is dedicated to the Way.
There are other scriptures that have been transmitted from generation to generation,
whether by laypeople or monastics.
They practice asceticism while relying heavily on their own skills;
they are self-important and look down upon others.
Third are the Vaiśyas, also called Viśas.
These are the four castes: first, the Vaiśyas, also called Śūdras or Chengdara, who are the agricultural caste;
second, the Kṣatriyas, of whom our Buddha, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, was a member.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"At the beginning of the formation of the Bhadrakalpa, there were as yet no sun or moon.
At that time, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to be born [in this world]."
All possess bodily radiance and travel through the air with ease;
there is no distinction between male and female, noble and base, or kin and stranger.
They ate the flavor of the earth that arises spontaneously.
Because they consumed this substance,
their bodily radiance faded and their supernormal powers perished.
As the mind of greed first sprouted,
they further consumed the flavors of earth-cakes, earth-skins, and earth-fat;
thus, all manner of evils converged.
When the forms of male and female first appeared,
the earth produced non-glutinous rice;
it was harvested in the morning and grew again by evening.
There were also no husks or chaff.
At that time, people’s greed increased,
and they all took large stores of wealth in advance.
Rice subsequently ceased to grow;
thereupon, each occupied their own fields and soil,
learning the arts of cultivation and sowing.
From this point on, villainy and theft flourished;
among them was one man who lacked the power of decisive judgment.
His appearance and character were magnificent and noble;
he was revered and trusted by the world,
and by common consensus, he was established as the leader of the people.

He was titled Mahāsammatarāja, which means "Great Lord of Universal Equality. Each person pledged to deliver taxes and provisions; this was the beginning of ancestral taxation. Therefore, he was given the clan name Kṣatriya, which means "Lord of the Land," signifying that when land and fields were first divided, there were disputes over them, and he was appointed to preside over them.
There are five distinct lineages of Buddhas; our Buddha Śākyamuni, throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
cultivated the causes of the six perfections and myriad practices,
manifesting either through the retribution of reality or through skillful transformation.
Each is named according to their respective lineage.
First is Gautama; in Sanskrit, it is correctly called Gautama.
Furthermore, it is said that *Gautamī* means "Supreme among the Earthly.
This refers to her being the most excellent among human beings on earth, excluding the devas.
Thus, a sutra states:
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, the Buddha was a king who abdicated his throne to become a disciple of the seer Gautama and practiced the Way.
He frequently dwelt and traveled within a certain garden.
He was killed by bandits;
the seer then enshrouded the corpse, took the blood,
and formed two lumps of clay.
Place it in a vessel and set it to one's left or right;
recite the mantra over it for a full ten months.
The left side transformed into a male;
the right side transformed into a female.
Thereupon, they were given a clan name.
Gautama was his original name.
The *Ikṣvāku-sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a wheel-turning monarch."
He was named Maheśvara.
His descendants succeeded one another,
totaling eighty-four thousand kings.
The last king was named Mahā-kuśa.
In his old age, having no son,
he entrusted the administration of the government to his ministers.
Having shaved his hair and left the household life,
he was known by the multitude as the Royal Seer (Rāja-ṛṣi).
Being extremely old, he was unable to walk or move about.
At that time, the disciples went out to beg for alms;
they then placed the royal seer in a grass basket and suspended it from a tree,
fearing harm from tigers and wolves.
A hunter saw him from afar, mistaking him for a white bird, and shot him dead.
His blood flowed onto the ground.
When the disciples returned and saw that their teacher had been killed, [they were overcome with grief].
They immediately prepared the body for burial; where the blood had dripped upon the ground, two stalks of sugarcane suddenly sprouted later on.
When scorched by the sun, they split open, and from one emerged a young boy.
She remained a maiden throughout her life.
When the minister heard of this, he went to fetch her and brought her back to the palace,
where he raised and nurtured her until she reached adulthood.
Because he was of royal lineage, he was subsequently established as king;
his clan name was Ikṣvāku, which began with him. Alternatively, in Sanskrit it is called [Ikṣvāku].
"Gautama" or "Kautamī"—
the two surnames mean "Most Victorious" in the language of China.
The *Jīngyīnshū* (Commentary on the Pronunciation of the Sūtras) states:
"They are all of the lineage of King Ikṣvāku.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (*Shùnzhènglǐlùn*) states:
Of the Gautama clan,
born from the light of the sun;
according to the *Trisūryavaṃśa-sūtra*, he was the son of King Ikṣvāku, not born from a womb.
Because it opens and unfolds when scorched by the sun, it is named "Sun-Seed" (Sūryagotra). The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"Those whose surname is 'Sun' are so called because they have departed from all darkness."
Because they produce radiance, I shall now examine these two sūtras: the former concerns the original causal conditions, while the latter concerns their merits.
As for the four Śākyas, they were the four princes exiled by King Ikṣvāku.
The first is named Flame-Face;
the second is named Golden Color;
the third is named Elephant Host.
The four named Nigrodha— translated in the Sui language as "separately formed"—
first arrived at the north of the Snowy Mountains and halted beneath a great tree with luxuriant branches and foliage;
for this reason, they were called Śāyikya.
The present term "Shaiyi-bi" (舍夷必) is a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit [Śrāvastī].
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Near the Śīta-vana forest to the north of the Snowy Mountains,
he built a city and established dwellings.
Furthermore, King Bimbisāra first asked the Buddha in which country he was born.
The Buddha said: "He was born in the country of Śākya;
now it is clear that the country must have derived its name from a tree, and the clan name followed that of the country. *Fayuan zhulin* states: [as cited above].
The Śākyas were a noble clan of the western region.
The five Śākya lineages originated from those four princes who, through their virtue, gathered people around them.
Within a few years,
it became a powerful nation;
his father, the king, then felt regret and remembered [his son].
He dispatched messengers with an imperial decree to summon his four sons, but they declined on the grounds of their transgressions and did not return.
The King, their father, then sighed three times and said:
"My son Śākyamuni—whose name in the language of China means 'Able One' (Nengren)—" as stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Śākyamuni: in the language of Qin, it means "able";
it is also translated as "straight."
That is to say, it is direct.
Therefore, I shall examine these two translations: the former proceeds from the person [of the Buddha] and the latter proceeds from the location; now I shall examine them.
All four princes were named Śākya.
Only the fourth, Nyagrodha, is my Buddha-ancestor.
According to the sutras,
Nyagrodha had a son named Kuru.
Kuru had a son named Gaurika.
Gaurika had a son named Siṃhahanu.
Siṃhahanu had four sons.
First, Śuddhodana;
second, Śuklodana;
third, Droṇodana.
The fourth was Amṛtodana (in Sanskrit, *Śuddhodana*),
which here means King Śuddhodana;
he was the father of the Buddha.
Regarding the surnames of those who have left the household life, the Kaiyuan Lu states that prior to the Qin and Jin dynasties,
those who entered the monastic order mostly followed the surname of their teacher.
Later, the Celestial-Spreading Śramaṇa Dao’an said:
"Those who shave their heads and dye their robes continue the lineage of Śākyamuni."
Thus, there would be no distinction between noble lineages;
it would be appropriate for all to be called Śākyas.
At that time, however, this was not yet the case.
Furthermore, the *Āgama* sūtras translated [into Chinese] state:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"The waters of the four great rivers flow into the ocean."
They no longer retained their original names,
but were all given the same name, Sāgara.
They were the sons of members of the four castes.
Having gone forth from the household life under the Buddha, with hair and beard shaved off and wearing the three dharma robes,
they no longer possess their original surnames.
It merely says, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya. The Mahīśāsaka-vinaya states:
"You bhikṣus have gone forth from among various classes of people."
They all abandoned their original surnames and were collectively called "sons of Śākya"; the current title "Śramaṇa Śākyaputra" likely originated from those who left the household life in India.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) also call themselves śramaṇas;
therefore, we now distinguish them by the character "Śākya" (釋).
Alternatively, it may be sufficient to simply use "Śākya."
If both parties are members of the Sangha,
then there is no need to state their names,
as they belong to the same Śākya clan.
Because they are Dharma-brothers.
As for the title "Śramaṇa," Master Zhaoshī says it is the general name for those who have left the household life.
In Sanskrit it is *śramaṇa*;
the character *man* (懣) is pronounced with a rising tone (*shang-sheng*).
In the language of Tang, it means "diligent and at rest," referring to one who diligently cultivates wholesome qualities.
Because it quiets all evils.
Furthermore, the Qin translation states:
"Diligent practice" means diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas and proceeding toward Nirvana.
Some call it *śramaṇa*, while others call it *sāṃmāna*;
these are merely differences in the dialects of the translators. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "Good Awakening. The *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states:
Because one is free from the mass of all fetters, one is called a śramaṇa. The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* states:
"One who has transcended defiled attachment is a śramaṇa. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
The mind has no attachment or delight;
it harbors no expectations for anything whatsoever,
and is thus able to liberate itself from all craving.
This is called a śramaṇa. The *Huashou jing* says:
"Like space, which has no contact or obstruction, it cannot be defiled by smoke or dust."
I say that the dharma of a śramaṇa is likewise free from defilement. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"A śramaṇa is so called because of his quiescence."
Because of being tamed,
because of receiving instruction,
and because of the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline.
Because it is according to reality,
because one attains liberation,
and because one is free from the thirty-eight factors.
Because his firm mind is unshakable like the earth,
because he protects the minds of both others and himself,
and because he is free from attachment to all forms and appearances.
Just as moving one's hand through the air meets no obstruction,
because he has accomplished such manifold dharmas,
he is called a śramaṇa. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
A śramaṇa is one who has abandoned affection and love,
leaving the household life to cultivate the Way.
He restrains his sense faculties,
remains unstained by external desires, maintains a heart of loving-kindness toward all,
and causes no harm whatsoever.
Encountering suffering, one does not grieve;
encountering joy, one does not rejoice.
One is able to endure like the earth. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
There are four kinds of śramaṇas.
The first is the śramaṇa who has excelled in the path,
namely the Buddha and others.
Second, the śramaṇa who speaks of the path,
meaning one who proclaims the true Dharma;
third, the śramaṇa who lives by the path.
This refers to those who cultivate the various categories of wholesome qualities.
There are four types of śramaṇas who defile the path;
"path" here refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. Those who practice such wrong conduct [are the first type].
If there were such a path,
yet one practices deviant conduct oneself,
one is not a vessel for the arising of the path.
Therefore, it is called "defiling the path.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When the Buddha first attained the Way, everyone in the world referred to him as 'the Great Śramaṇa.'"
"Bhikṣu" in the language of India is called "Bhikṣu";
in the language of Qin, it means "mendicant."
That is to say, above, one begs the Dharma from the Buddhas to nourish and benefit the life of wisdom;
below, one begs for food from donors.
Benefiting the physical body. Master Zhaoluo said:
"There are three names for cause and effect.
The first is 'Terrifying Māra'."
This is because at the time of renunciation, the palace of Māra shook;
thus, upon reaching the fruit [of Arhatship], one is called a "slayer of the thief.
It is said that those who renounce possess right faith and the right cause.
Arousing a courageous and resolute mind,
one seeks the great Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit and vows to deliver all sentient beings.
Only those with a truly great mind can shake the palaces of Māra.
Among the two causes [for the name], he is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu).
In terms of the fruit, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

Among the three causes, he is called "Destroyer of Evil," which refers to observing the precepts as the destruction of evil; upon reaching the fruit, this is called "Non-arising. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Because he is able to destroy the afflictions,
he is called a bhikṣu;
he destroys the notion of a self.
Cultivating precept, concentration, and wisdom,
they cross over the four currents of the triple existence and dwell securely in the path of fearlessness.
Therefore, he is called a bhikṣu. The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* states:
"Because he has shattered the storehouse of ignorance, he is called a bhikṣu. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"As for the bhikṣu..."

The nature of a bhikṣu consists in abandoning the household life to enter the homeless state, being fully endowed with the commonality of the prātimokṣa vows, exerting diligent effort regarding one’s physical form, guarding oneself out of fear of the evil destinies, and being restrained from causing harm. As a verse in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
Do not recklessly harm hands or feet;
be moderate in speech and act in accordance with what you practice;
always delight in maintaining a concentrated mind.
This is called a true bhikṣu. A verse from the *Saṃyukta Āgama* says:
"One who is called a bhikṣu is not so merely by begging for food."
One who upholds the dharma of a householder—
how can such a person be called a bhikṣu?
Regarding virtues and faults, [what is his standing]?
Having abandoned all things and practicing correct conduct,
their minds are free from fear;
such a person is called a bhikṣu [endowed with] the Great Majestic Virtue Dhāraṇī.
There was an elder named Selection who left the household life to become a monk under the Buddha.
When his hair had been shaved, the Venerable Sāṇavāsa called out,
"Householder, choose! He replied,
"I have now gone forth, shaved my hair, and become a bhikṣu."
"That is not the mark of an elder. Then Pāṇḍaka said,
"One is not called a bhikṣu merely because of having shaved one's hair."
Then he spoke in verse, saying:
"If one cuts off desire and hope, and further cuts off all outflows until they are exhausted,
then all phenomena will be free from hope."
It cannot be said that there exists any phenomenon that accords with and leads toward nirvāṇa,
or that accords with and leads toward disenchantment and detachment.
Entering faith and reaching the other shore—
this constitutes being a bhikṣu.
There are four kinds of bhikṣus.
First, the bhikṣu who has reached the ultimate path,
namely the arhat;
second, the bhikṣu who demonstrates the path.
This refers to the noble ones who have attained the three fruits,
and the bhikṣus practicing the path who have attained the three fruits,
as well as those who are candidates for the first fruit.
The fourth are bhikṣus who defile the path;
that is, ordinary persons who have broken the precepts and ordinary persons who maintain the precepts, because they follow the dharma of faith and following the precepts,
and thus necessarily rank below those who receive the path.
Question: Is a bhikṣu who has defiled the path worthy of being a field of merit? Answer:
The Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra states that although a bhikṣu who has defiled the path has broken his precepts, he has not broken his views.
Although he has broken his application, he has not broken his intention; thus, he possesses the right view that believes in cause and effect. Such is the meaning.
The ninety-six kinds of pleasures found among the non-Buddhist outsiders do not exist here;
rather, it is simply that the donor conceives right faith toward them and does not give rise to aversion.
One naturally generates great merit.
"Bhikṣu" is a term from the Sanskrit language;
it is the name of a grass from the Western Heavens (India).
Because it possesses five virtues,
it is used as a metaphor for those who have left the household life.
An ancient master said:
The reason why the *Bhikṣu-sūtra* was not translated [into Chinese] is that it contains five meanings.
The first is that its essential nature is supple and soft.
The first metaphor illustrates how those who have left the household life can subdue the coarseness of body and speech.
The second, the spreading of trailing vines,
illustrates how those who have left the household life transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in an unceasing succession.
Third, its fragrance is heard afar;
this is a metaphor for how the precepts and virtue of those who have left the household life are fragrant and renowned among the multitude. Fourth, it can cure pain;
this is a metaphor for how those who have left the household life are able to sever the poisonous harm of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fifth, one does not turn one's back to the sun;
this is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, as they always face the Buddha-sun. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ekottara-karmavastu* states:
"There was a bhikṣu who was eighty years old and had completed sixty years of summer retreats (*varṣa*)."
If one has never read or recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra and does not understand its meaning.
This is called the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* for elder and junior bhikṣus;
it is the very *Śīla-mātṛkā*.
This is merely an illustration of the general principle.
The term *saṃgha* is rendered in full as *saṃgha* in the Sanskrit language;
in the Tang language it means "assembly," and is now abbreviated as "Seng. The *Madhyama Āgama* asks:
"What is called an assembly?"
Answer: There are those of various surnames and various names who shave off their hair and beards and don the saffron robes.
Having attained supreme faith, they left the household life to follow the Buddha and study the Path;
this is called the *saṃgha*. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Those who are equal in precepts, equal in view, and equal in wisdom—this assembly is the *saṃgha*. The *Nanshan chao* states: [as above].
With four or more persons,
one can uphold the noble Dharma and accomplish the aforementioned tasks.
This is called the Saṃgha.
The meaning of "Saṃgha" is harmony and union.
As for what is meant by "harmony and union":
There are two kinds. First,
harmony by principle (*yukti-sāmagrī*),
which refers to the fact that they equally realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are six distinct meanings for these two types of harmony:
first, harmony of precepts through collective practice;
second, harmony of views through shared understanding.
Third, they dwell together in harmony of body.
Fourth, they share equally in the harmony of benefit.
Fifth, they maintain harmony of speech without contention.
Sixth, their minds are harmonious and joyful.
The *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:
"Generally, four or more persons are designated as the Saṃgha."
Now, when even a single person is called a "sangha," it is because they are designated by the name of the multitude;
it is just as when twelve thousand five hundred people constitute an army.
A single person is also called an "army.
Kang Senghui’s commentary on the *Fajing jing* (*Dharmadarśana-sūtra*) states:
"Ordinary people are greedily attached to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*)."
It is like a starving man who greedily craves food and knows no satiety;
now the Sage has severed craving and eliminated the famine of the six sense-faculties.
Therefore, he is titled "The One Who Eliminates Famine" (Arhat). The *Fenbie Gongde Lun* states:
"Ordinary people suffer from the famine of sensual desire;
because a bhikṣu eliminates this notion of craving-famine, he is so called."
The *Dashi zhuzhuan duanjie jing* (Sutra on the Ten Stages of the Teacher’s Severance of Bonds) states:
"One who is called a 'Teacher' causes the various classes of sentient beings [to attain liberation]."
Because he demonstrates the true path. The *Huashou jing* (Flower-Head Sūtra) says:
"Because he can preach for others the path that is without birth and death, he is called a Guide.
The *Fobao'en jing* (Sūtra on the Requital of the Buddha’s Kindness) says:
The Great Guide reveals the path of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra so that beings may attain the unconditioned,
eternal bliss. As stated in the *Mahādharanī-dharmolkā-sūtra*:
Because one is able to not regress from the path to enlightenment and does not sever the path to enlightenment,
one is called a "Guide. As stated in the *Sārthavāha-devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
Mañjuśrī replied: "One who,
having established themselves in this path,
is able to bring sentient beings to maturity is called a 'Guide'."
Therefore, he is called the "Guide.
The *Zushi Baolin Zhuan* (The Record of the Jewel Forest of the Patriarchs) states that Yang Xuanzhi was the Prefect of Qicheng.
He asked Bodhidharma,
"In the Western Land, what is the meaning of the term 'Patriarch' (zu) as it is handed down?
Bodhidharma replied:
One who clarifies the Buddha-mind school and whose practice accords with understanding is called a Patriarch.
From the time the Master Bodhidharma came from the West until the Great Master Huineng of Caoxi, [this lineage was maintained].
Six individuals may be designated as ancestral teachers (*pūrvācārya*).
The *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Susthitamati* states:
A devaputra asked Mañjuśrī: [text continues]
"What kind of bhikṣu is named a dhyāna-master?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Regarding all dharmas..."
One should contemplate in a single line:
namely, non-arising.
If one knows it thus, [one attains liberation].
He was thus named Chan Master.
Furthermore, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be grasped.
What dharma would he not grasp?
That is to say, not grasping at this world or future worlds;
not grasping at the three realms up to all phenomena— meaning that one does not grasp at anything at all because all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
When sentient beings do not grasp in this way, they are called *dhyāna-masters*.

Because they do not grasp even the slightest thing, nor do they non-grasp, and because they find nothing at all in any phenomena (*sarva-dharma*), they are without recollection (*asmṛti*). If there is no recollection, then there is no cultivation; if there is no cultivation, then there is no realization. For this reason, they are called *dhyāna-masters*.
The *Sutra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom on Good Spiritual Friends* states:
"One who can expound emptiness and signlessness..."
Non-action,
the dharmas that are neither arising nor ceasing, and all-knowledge.

"To fulfill the eight limbs, namely: faith."
Observing the precepts,
practicing generosity,
and listening to the Dharma.
Uphold it,
understand its meaning,
and practice according to what has been taught.
The term *upāsikā* is a feminine form;
it is also said that the name and meaning of *upāsikā* are the same as those previously explained.
The seven assemblies refer to bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās,
and śrāmaṇeras.
The śrāmaṇerikā constitutes the five groups of those who have left the household life;
the upāsaka and upāsikā constitute the two groups of those who remain in the household. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Those who are able to maintain the Buddha-dharma consist of these seven groups in the world, through whom the fruits of the path of the three vehicles continue without interruption."
Taking the Prātimokṣa as the root. The Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra states:
"The seven classes [of practitioners] are:
first, the bhikṣu."
1. Bhikṣuṇīs; 2. Śikṣamāṇās;
3. Śrāmaṇeras (in the language of Tang, *qínsè nán*, meaning "diligent male," i.e., śrāmaṇeras or novices); 4. [Śrāmaṇerīs].
Fifth, śrāmaṇerikā, which in the language of Tang means "female novice" (i.e., a śrāmaṇerī).
Sixth, upāsaka. Seventh, upāsikā.
"Virtue" (dào-dé) refers to the designation for the Eightfold Noble Path being fully endowed both internally and externally with the seven branches of ethical discipline. The *Lunheng* states:
"To achieve renown is called 'the Way' (dào);
to establish one's person is called 'virtue' (dé)."
"Renown and virtue" means "reality.
When reality is established, renown follows it.
As Confucius said:
What is esteemed is the name that accords with reality.
"Virtue" (de) means "attainment" (de);
it refers to what one has internally attained within oneself.
Externally, one gains the favor of others;
internally, one is always without loss.
To combine these and speak of them—this is the *Āgama Sūtra*.
After the passage beginning with "Having called Śāriputra," it says:
"For a monk of renown and virtue... Master Jiao’s Preface to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan xu*) states:
'One of meager virtue who happens to be timely is renowned but not eminent; one of real virtue whose brilliance remains hidden is eminent but not renowned.'"
"Monastery" (saṃghārāma) is the Sanskrit term for *zhùchù* (residence).
It is also called *saṃgharāma*.
This is called the Saṅghārāma (Garden of the Assembly).
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*,
it was King Bimbisāra who first offered the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden.
A garden is a place where things grow and flourish;
the disciples of the Buddha dwell therein,
taking the sense of "growing and flourishing" to mean the fundamental path and the holy fruit.
Some call it *vihāra*,
which here means a place for wandering and dwelling;
"temple" (*si*) is the Chinese designation for it.
The *Shiming* states:
"Si" means "succession.
It refers to those who manage affairs.
These were successively inherited within its lineage.
Thus, the Son of Heaven had nine temples.
In the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the year Dingmao, the Buddha-dharma first arrived.
There were two Indian monks, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who arrived at Luoyang carrying scriptures and images on white horses;
by imperial decree, they were accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Honglu (Minister of Reception) was established as the Sibusi (Bureau of Guests).
Hu Guang’s commentary explains:
"Hong" refers to a great sound.
The *lu* (proclamation) is used to transmit sounds and assist in guiding the nine guests. In the Qin dynasty,
there was the Office of the Director of Guests (*Dianke*).
The Han dynasty followed this precedent.
It was renamed Tongwen Temple during the Tang dynasty.
Then, in the eleventh year, the Wuchen year, [it was further altered].
An imperial decree was issued to construct a separate monastery outside the Yong Gate,

Sun Quan of Wu established Jianchu Monastery;
this was the beginning.
"Yuan" (cloister) is called *lāma* in Sanskrit.
The *Yinyi* (Phonetic and Semantic Explanations) of the *Fayuan Jing* (Scriptures from the Garden of Dharma) produced in the Tang Dynasty. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
*Paryanta*; this is called a surrounding corridor or courtyard.
Daochang initially stated:
"A place for leisurely and tranquil cultivation of the Way is called a *doichang* (place of the Way)."
The Sui Emperor Yang issued an edict to change the names of all monastic residences to "Daochang" (Dharma-grounds) and "Jingshe" (Vihāras).
The *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni) states: [as cited above].
A place where the mind of cessation dwells is called a *vihāra* (jing-she). The *Yiwen leiju* states:
"It is not because the building itself is exquisite;
rather, it is truly because it is the dwelling place of those who have refined their practice."
The *Zhao ti zeng hui ji* (Record of the Radiance Increasing of the Zhao ti) states that in Sanskrit it is called *stūpa*,
which in the Tang language means "property of the Sangha of the four quarters.
However, this is merely a scribal error.
Expand it to form the *zhāo* (invocation);
remove the *dòu* and *shē*,
and retain the *tí*.
Therefore, it is called "Zhao ti" (Cāturdīśa),
which refers to the monasteries currently maintained by the ten directions. This is it.
Sengfang Yunlin says: "Fang" (坊) refers to a district or ward.
Master Yuan says: [The following].
The Monastery of the Neighborhood (Lan-mo-yuan) is also known as the Deer Park (Lu-yuan), located in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
It was there that the Buddha first attained enlightenment.
The place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned and the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, were delivered;
this Kukkutārāma was built by King Aśoka in the kingdom of Magadha.
This was the monastery where the Bhikṣu Mahādeva, the leader of the Mahāsāṃghika school of the Hīnayāna, went forth.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, many eminent and virtuous bhikṣus resided at Kukkutārāma.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) concerning the Wild Goose Pagoda states:
Long ago, there was a bhikṣu who saw a flock of wild geese flying overhead and remarked jokingly that they knew the proper time.
Suddenly, a wild goose plummeted down and died of its own accord.
The assembly said, "This goose has offered a warning;
we should commemorate its profound virtue."
Thereupon, the wild geese were buried and a stupa was erected.
"Cetiya" is the Sanskrit term for *zhiti*; it is also transliterated as *zhidi* or *zhidu*.
It is also called *zhidi* or *zhiduō*.
All are translated as "spiritual shrines" (lingmiao). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"That which contains no relics is called a *caitya* (zhiti), and it is also termed a place for extinguishing evil and generating goodness."
*Brahmā-kṣetra*: "Brahmā" means purity. According to the *Jīngyīn* (Sound of the Sūtras), the Sanskrit term is *raśmi*, which here means "flute."
Now, "kṣetra" (刹) is abbreviated;
it refers to the banner-pillar (*dhvajastaṃbha*). The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"If a śramaṇa exerts himself with diligent effort within this monastery..."
Upon attaining even a single dharma,
one should immediately raise a banner and announce to the four quarters:
"Now there dwells here a person who has few desires and is content."
The *Naiyuan Dadei Neidian Lu* states that when the Kasmirian meditation master Fashou first arrived in Dunhuang,
he erected a meditation pavilion on a secluded and open site.
He planted a thousand *nai* trees;
those who flocked to him were like clouds, and his assembly was magnificent.
According to some, this was the Golden Land.
The Golden Field (Kanakakheda).
This is the city of Śrāvastī,
where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada spread gold over the ground.
He purchased Prince Jeta’s garden to build a vihāra and invited the Buddha to reside there.

Regarding the Lotus Society: in the past, during the Jin dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Huiyuan, whom Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty posthumously titled the Dharma Master Da Jue (Great Awakening).
A native of Yanmen, he resided at Donglin Temple on the Tiger Creek of Mount Lu.

He invited eminent scholars such as Liu Yimin, Zong Bing, Lei Cizong, Zhang Ye, Zhang Quan, and Zhou Xuzhi to form an assembly for the cultivation of the pure practices of the Western Paradise; that monastery was planted with many white lotuses.
Furthermore, because the land of Amitābha Buddha admits people in nine successive grades according to their lotus flowers, it is called the "Lotus Society" (Lian-she). Some say:
It is praised that these members of the community are not defiled by the mud of fame and profit;
they are thus named after being likened to the lotus flower.
Some say:
Master Huiyuan had a disciple named Faya who carved wood into twelve-petaled lotus flowers and planted them in water.
By means of a mechanical device,
every time a single leaf is folded constitutes one *kāla*;
it does not differ from the water-clock (*ghaṭikā*) in its precision.
Because ritual recitation was thereby made to never lose its proper timing, it was named after this;
it is also called the "Pure Society" (Jingshe).
This refers to Prince Wenxuan of Jingling during the Southern Qi dynasty.
This is because it compiles the pure conduct for both monastics and laypeople.
Now, as for the "society" (śā),
it is established following the principles of the spring and autumn seasons.
The fifth *wù* (geng) day is called the "She Day" (*shèrì*).
Farmers throughout the world gather for a festival to pray for a bountiful harvest.
The *Jingchu ji* states:
The four people together formed the Society of the Combined Ropes.
The *Baïhùtōng* (*White Tiger General Exposition*) asks:
"Why does the King have a She altar?"
The world seeks lands that bestow blessings and rewards.
Yet humans cannot eat without land;
because the earth is so vast, it is impossible to pay reverence to it all.
Earth was enclosed to establish the altar of the community (she), and now the followers of the Śākya tradition likewise form bonds of devotion.
Monastics and laypeople alike establish the Dharma to pray for blessings and seek rebirth in the Pure Land;
such pure lands are vast and numerous.
Having sought everywhere and found only mental distraction, he resolutely pointed to the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) as the place for his spirit to dwell;
thus it was named the Lotus Society (Lian-she) and the Pure Society (Jing-she).
"Āraṇya" is the Sanskrit term;
it is also called *āraṇya* or *aranyaka*.
The Tang translation says: "the place of non-contention.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says: "a quiet and secluded place. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* says:
"a tranquil and secluded place. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: [a quiet and secluded place].
Regarding dwelling in seclusion, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"An araṇya is so called because it is free from all worldly distractions. The *Dvādaśa-dhūta-guṇa-sūtra* states: [as follows].
The Buddha said: "The Aranya is praised by all Buddhas of the ten directions; immeasurable merits are all born from it. Master Zhaò said:
"Anger and contention arise in the midst of a multitude."
Non-contention arises from dwelling in empty and quiet places.
The Buddha praised abiding in an araṇya. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"In an araṇya location, one is solitary and still, with no people to cause disturbance."
Alms are easily obtained there; it is neither too far nor too near; it abounds in trees, flowers, and fruits; it has pure and excellent water; and its cave-dwellings are secure.
Regarding the term *araṇya*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: [text follows]
A secluded place should be at least two *li* away;
the further, the better.
One *krośa* from the village—this is translated as "the sound of a drum. The Vinaya states:
Five hundred *dhanus* from the village;
a *dhanus* is equivalent to a *zhen* (尋).
This is the custom of the Western Heavens (India).
Generally, four *hasta* constitute one *dhanus*.
A *hasta* is eighteen inches long, totaling seven feet and two inches. Five hundred *dhanus* constitute one *krośa*, which accumulates to three thousand six hundred inches.
This amounts to six hundred paces,
which is equivalent to two *li*.
Regarding the etymological explanation of the term "ān" (*āma*), it says:
A hut made of grass is called an *ān*.
It is "ān" because it covers itself;
it is an *ān* because it shelters itself.

In the Western Heavens (India), monks and laypeople who practice the Way mostly reside in hermitages; among the gentlemen of this land (China) as well, there are those who dwell in hermitages, such as Xianrong Xu.
The *Book of Jin* states that Tao Yan, at the age of fifteen, ceased eating grain and lived in a grass hut.
A *ge* (spear) can accommodate one’s body. The *Yishizhuan* (Biographies of Recluse Scholars) states that Tao Qian lived in a thatched hut (*peng’an*).
The *Shenxianzhuan* (Biographies of Transcendents) states that Jiao Guang lived in a grass hut (*cao’an*).
The name "Grass Hall" (*Caotang*) first gained its renown through Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Prior to this, since the fall of Chang'an under the Han and its restoration by the Qin, more than three hundred years had passed.
The imperial palaces and marketplaces lay desolate and abandoned;
although there were several monasteries, those who turned toward them were few.
During the reign of Yao Xing, Kumārajīva—
whose name is translated as "Child-Longevity" (Tóngshòu)—
constructed a hall within the Great Monastery and thatched its roof with grass; it was for this reason that the hall was so named.
The abbot’s quarters (bǎngzhàng) is the principal residence of the monastery.

It originated during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, when by imperial decree Li Yibiao of the Weiwu Temple and Wang Xuance, former Magistrate of Huangshui in Rongzhou, were dispatched as envoys to the Western Regions.
Arriving at the city of Vaiśālī,
about four li to the northeast was the room where the layman Vimalakīrti manifested illness in his residence.
The ruins were constructed by stacking stones.
King Ce personally measured them with his handboard from side to side and front to back, finding they spanned ten *hù*;
thus, it was named Fangzhang (Ten-Fan).
The *Fáng shì míng* (Explanation of the Name "Room") states: "A room (*fáng*) is so called because it is on the side;
it is located at both sides of the hall. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "The bhikṣu Pāvārika requested permission for bhikṣus to accept the gift of a dwelling (*vihāra*)."
The Buddha then granted permission. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"A 'room' may belong to the Saṃgha—such as a meditation hall or quarters—or it may belong to a single individual—such as those currently held by individual abbots within a monastery. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a room has just been completed..."
There was a newly ordained bhikṣu whose virtue of precepts was pure.

Having entered this room, once the donor’s mind of faithful giving had been fulfilled—even if various dwellings were adorned with high and wide magnificence—if a bhikṣu of pure precepts uses them for even a brief moment, the donor’s grace is fully realized; for the precepts are not a worldly phenomenon.
The *Yantang Shanjian Lü* states:
"At the Great Forest, Vaiśālī constructed a hall for the Buddha;
its shape was like that of a wild goose."
All were fully provided.
The *Āgama Sūtra* states that the Buddha entered his meditation chamber and sat in quietude (*kāyotsarga*).
Furthermore, it is also called a "Chan-zhai" (meditation fast).
"Zhai" carries the meaning of solemnity and stillness;
it is like how, within Confucianism, a quiet room is referred to as a "shu-zhai" (study).
Alternatively, it refers to a place where officials or clerks maintain quiet governance,
which is called a "prefectural study" (jùnzhāi).
As for the term "Xiao Temple" (Xiàosì), it is now commonly used to refer to monastic residences.
It must have been because Emperor Wu of Liang had named a temple after his own surname.

When Li Jue of the Tang dynasty purchased the temple plaque from Liang Wu’s temple in Huainan, he obtained the large-scale flying-robic (feibok) calligraphy of Xiao Ziyun inscribing the character "Xiao.
He took it back to his residence in Luoyang and enshrined it in a small pavilion, which he named "Xiao Qi."
The learned and virtuous gentleman further corrected it.
In the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, Tripiṭaka Master Yijing’s commentary states:
"In the West, a Buddha hall is called a *gandhakūṭī*."
This is called the "Fragrant Chamber" (xiāngshì) rather than being termed a "Buddha Hall" (fótáng) or "Buddha Temple" (fódiàn).
This is likely because one does not wish to directly touch the venerable countenance; furthermore, the term "temple" (diàn) is a convention specific to this region.
This refers to the fish-tail design placed upon the upper [part].
The term "tail" (wei) is now colloquially called "fish-lip" (yu-wen), which is a corruption. Jiu Guzi said:
When the Hall of the Piercing Beam (Bailiang Dian) in the Han dynasty was struck by a calamity—a celestial fire—a Yue shaman offered a ritual technique:
he took the tail of a *shu* fish and placed it atop the hall to ward off the disaster.
Now, this [present phenomenon] is likewise a portent.
If one adds iron to the tip of the ancient ritual arrow (*wei*) to form the shape of water-weeds,
it is popularly called a "crow-cluster" (*zǎn niǎo*).
The *Fengsu tong* states:
Ancient halls were frequently carved with lotus flowers, water lilies, and water chestnut leaves—aquatic plants used for the purpose of suppressing fire.
Regarding the method for constructing a *saṃghārāma*, it accords with the ten chapters on the construction of monasteries composed by Dharma Master Lingyu.
Furthermore, to clarify the method for constructing a monastery according to the authentic teachings:
in order to avoid censure and entanglement,
one should stay away from nunneries as well as markets and government offices.
This is so that there may be nothing to be destroyed hereafter. Nanshan said:
"Laypeople do not understand the Dharma."
The monastic community should provide clear guidance.
Regarding the deities who protect the monastery, the *Sūtra of the Seven Buddhas* states:
"There are eighteen deities who protect the monastery."
First, the beautiful voice;
second, the Brahma-voice;
third, the celestial drum.
Fourth is praising the sublime;
fifth is praising the beautiful;
sixth is polishing the sublime.
Seventh, Thunderous Sound;
eighth, Lion;
ninth, Wondrous Praise.
10. Brahma-sound;
11. human voice;
12. Buddha’s attendant.
Thirteen: Praising Virtue;
Fourteen: Broad Eyes;
Fifteen: Wondrous Eyes.
16. Pervasive hearing;
17. Pervasive seeing;
18. Universal seeing. Master Daoshi said:
Since this monastery is protected by the eighteen deities,
those who reside here should likewise exert themselves and must not be indolent or commit transgressions.
I fear it would invite retribution in this present life; generally, whenever there is a painting of a great deity on the walls of a temple, it is this very deity.
Someone once asked: "Within this world, there are countless monasteries."
Question: How is it that eighteen deities alone are able to provide universal protection?
Answer: All deities possess countless retinues;
thus, there is no contradiction in assigning them specific roles for protection.
Regarding the monks' management of monasteries, according to the Vinaya, the Buddha’s great disciples all personally managed their own monasteries;
for example, Mahākāśyapa personally trampled the mud and so forth.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"The great disciples have already exhausted their outflows and fetters;
for what reason do they remain so anxious and occupied with worldly affairs?"
The answer is: there are five reasons: first, to repay the Buddha’s kindness;
second, to nurture and develop the Buddha-dharma;
third, to eliminate the self-conceit of ordinary and inferior beings.
Fourth, it is for the sake of subduing arrogance and pride in future disciples;
fifth, it is for the sake of inspiring future meritorious deeds.
Regarding the Three Gates (sammôn) of a temple:
why is it that even when there is only a single gate, it is still referred to as the "Three Gates"?
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The great palace has the three gates of liberation as its entrance.
The great palace is a metaphor for the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) and nirvāṇa.
The three gates of liberation are the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā-mukha), the gate of signlessness (animitta-mukha), and [the gate of wishlessness].
The Gate of Non-action:
This monastery is where those who maintain the precepts and cultivate the Way reside in order to seek the attainment of Nirvana; thus, they enter by way of these three gates.
Regarding "leaving home, leaving home, leaving home," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The householder is beset by vexations, as if dwelling within a dusty abode."
Having left the household life,
one dwells in seclusion as if in empty space;
therefore, one should relinquish everything regarding well-spoken teachings.
In the Vinaya, it is said that those with right faith leave the household life to enter the homeless state. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The household is a causal condition for the afflictions;
indeed, one who has left the household..."
In order to extinguish defilements and entanglements, one should distance oneself from them.
"Difficult, difficult" (nán-nán)—the second character is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
There was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Yaśas who asked Śāriputra,
"In the Dharma and Vinaya of the Noble Ones, what is difficult to do?"
Śāriputra said,
"Only leaving the household life is difficult.
He asked, "What makes it difficult?"
Answer: It is difficult to find those who delight [in the Dharma].
Question: In what way?
Answer: It is difficult to always delight in cultivating the wholesome.
Question: What is called wholesome dharma?
Answer: It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, for one who has gone forth from the household life.
By practicing this path,
one will before long swiftly attain the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava) through the Eightfold Noble Path:
right speech and right action.
Right livelihood—
these three belong to the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
because in the Hīnayāna, ethical discipline is held to be primary.
Right concentration,
right effort,
and right mindfulness.
These three belong to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since concentration is attained by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they follow in that order.
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
These two belong to wisdom (*prajñā*), because wisdom arises based on concentration (*samādhi*). The *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyuktāgama) of the Qin period states:
Now, those who have left the household life are said to have attained what is difficult to attain;
yet, if they give rise to an evil mind, [they fall].
It is not called "difficult to obtain.
Regarding the fact that leaving the household life takes faith as its primary basis, the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states:
The Buddha said:
If a person possesses faith,
they can enter the great ocean of my Dharma and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
Amoghasiddhi shaved his head and donned the dyed robes;
yet, if one lacks faith,
such a person cannot enter my great ocean of the Dharma.
Like a withered tree that does not produce flowers or fruit, one does not attain the fruits of the śramaṇa;
though one has shaved one's head, donned the dyed robes,
and recited various sūtras.
Able to raise objections and able to provide answers,
yet within the Buddha-dharma,
one finds nothing at all through emptiness.
For this reason, the Buddha-dharma is "good in the beginning" because of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"There are four kinds of faith."
First is the root of faith,
which consists in delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma.
Second is faith that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit, and thus constantly mindful of approaching, making offerings to, and revering him.
They initiate roots of goodness because they aspire to seek all-knowledge;
third, they believe that the Dharma brings great benefit.
Because they constantly contemplate and practice the various *pāramitās*.

The Sangha of those with the fourfold faith is able to correctly practice for their own benefit and the benefit of others, as they always delight in drawing near to the assembly of Bodhisattvas to seek and learn the practice of *tathatā*. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
Faith has three distinctions: first, faith in actual existence, which refers to profound conviction and acceptance regarding the reality and principles of all phenomena;
second, faith in excellence, which refers to profound conviction and delight regarding the true virtues of the Triple Gem.

Third is the conviction in capability, which refers to having deep faith that within all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas there is the power to attain and accomplish them, thereby giving rise to aspiration. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Faith is like a hand, for it is able to grasp wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "leaving home and transcending the five destinies," Master Kumārajīva’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"Ordinary persons are able to transcend the four miserable realms."
One cannot escape from the realm of heavenly beings (*deva-gati*).
To leave the household life and seek cessation (*nirodha*) is to transcend the five destinies; this cessation is *nirvāṇa*. Sengzhao says:
The five paths of rebirth are not the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "joyful upon leaving the household," Shi [Daoan] said:
"Joy is of two kinds."
First, there is the natural joy and anticipation regarding the merits of the present life;
second, there is the constant peace and gladness of mind upon attaining nirvana. Sengzhao says:
"Turbulence and disorder arise from excessive seeking."
Sorrow and suffering arise from insufficiency;
for one who has left the household life and possesses few desires,
such disturbances cease to exist.
Because the Way and its teachings are fully internalized,
his joy is overflowing.
Regarding the "Three Dharmas of Leaving Home," Śīkṣānanda says:
There are generally three dharmas for those who have left the household life:
first, the observance of the precepts;
second, meditative concentration.
Third is wisdom.
Upholding the precepts can subdue the afflictions and cause their power to diminish.
Meditative concentration can obstruct the afflictions,
just as a mountain to the right blocks a flowing stream;
wisdom can extinguish the afflictions.
Ultimately, there is nothing remaining... In the "Preface to the Great Precepts" by Dharma Master Dao’an, it is said:
"The World-Honored One established three categories of the teaching:
first, the Vinaya (precepts)."
Second is meditative concentration;
third is wisdom.
These three are the gateways to the ultimate Way.
Nirvana is the essential gateway;
the precepts are the Mojiang sword that severs the three evil paths;

Even if I were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, I could not exhaustively explain it.
Second, regarding the kindness of sentient beings:
Since beginningless time,
all sentient beings have transmigrated through the five realms of existence.
We have been each other's parents;
because each has bestowed great kindness,
there is the third [type of] kingly kindness.
Their merit is most supreme;
though born among humans,
they attain great sovereignty.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three constantly use their power to protect and sustain the boundaries of the kingdom.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth all belong to the king. Therefore,
the Great Sage King transforms them through the True Dharma.
It can cause all sentient beings to be entirely at peace and happy. A later translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In the land there is a sovereign king."
All shall obtain peace and security. Therefore,
the King of Men is the very foundation of peace and happiness for all sentient beings.
Whether lay or ordained, those who cultivate their minds with diligent self-restraint all rely upon a righteous state to maintain their practice,
thereby propagating and disseminating the teaching.
If there were no royal power,
meritorious practices would not be accomplished,
and the Dharma would perish without remainder.
How much more so, then, could it benefit and rescue others?
For this reason,
all the merit one cultivates—
One-sixth [of the land] shall always belong to the king.
May the mountain of the King’s merit be lofty, firm, and indestructible. The *Satyasiddhi-sūtra* says:
The king is the parent of the people.
He governs and protects sentient beings through the Dharma so that they may dwell in peace and happiness. Furthermore, when performing prostrations to the Buddha:
May the gods, dragons, and spirits always make this vow:
may the winds and rains be timely,
and may the civil and military officials be harmonious.
Regarding those who constantly occupy positions of emolument and rank,
the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"As for great ministers..."
This is a vital stronghold of the state.
Agriculture is the source of human sustenance; if the state loses its stronghold, it falls into peril;
if people are deprived of food, they die.
Furthermore, because the Buddha-dharma has been entrusted to kings and ministers,
one must constantly fix the mind upon them and offer prayers for their well-being.
Regarding the fourth [point], the grace of the Triple Gem:
The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma,
and Sangha possesses immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations.
Bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings without even a moment’s rest. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgata..."
The most supreme within the three realms,
you deliver us from birth and death;
this kindness is difficult to repay.
If one possesses a profound mind toward the Buddha-dharma and attains indestructible faith, this is called repaying kindness. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Throughout countless kalpas, the Tathāgata..."
He toiled and suffered for the sake of sentient beings.
Why do those in the world not repay the Great Teacher’s kindness? (From the *Baoen jing*).
Parents are the most supreme field of merit within the triple world. The Vinaya-vinīścaya states:
"Parents undergo great toil and hardship for the sake of their children."
Protecting, sustaining,
and nurturing them by providing nourishment with milk; even if one were to carry one's mother on one shoulder and one's father on the other shoulder.
Even if one were to exhaust oneself in vain for a hundred kalpas,
or provide various offerings of the seven treasures to bring about wealth and happiness,
one would still not have repaid the kindness of one's parents.
If their parents lack faith, he causes them to give rise to it;
if they lack ethical discipline,
he causes them to abide in the precepts.
If one is naturally stingy, they are made to practice generosity;
if one lacks wisdom,
they are made to give rise to wisdom.
If you can act in this way, only then may it be called repaying their kindness. The *Acintyaprabhāsa-sūtra* says:
"Neither food and drink nor jewels can repay the kindness of one's parents."
To guide them toward the True Dharma is to provide for one's two parents. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus to provide for their parents with all their heart and throughout their entire lives."
It is said that failing to make offerings results in a grave offense; furthermore, it is stated:

"I have authorized five persons who, even if they are extremely corrupt in their precepts, should still be honored—namely, one's mother, father, preceptor (upādhyāya), and the teacher from whom one receives the precepts (ācārya)."
The preceptor,
as well as the sick person,
and furthermore, it is said, the renunciant.
One should provide offerings and support to one's parents;
as for items other than the three robes, they may be obtained either by requesting them from a donor or by receiving them as a benefit from the Saṃgha.
Or he may provide half of his own regular portion of food for the Sangha; or,
if he subsists on alms, he may give from within his own meal that fills his belly.
One should take half [of one's merit] to provide for one's parents.
The *Zhongxin jing* (Sutra on the Central Mind) says:
The Buddha said, "Those who know the kindness of their teachers..."
When seeing the teacher, one serves him;
when not seeing him, one contemplates his instructions and admonitions,
just as a filial son thinks of his parents.
Just as a person thinks of food, drink, and so forth, the *Mahāvaipulya-acintya-viṣaya-sūtra* states:
"One should make offerings to one's parents and preceptors."
And toward those in the world who have once bestowed benefit upon us,
those who rely on their kindness should redouble their thoughts of gratitude and repay that kindness.
Why is this? Because one who recognizes kindness,
even while remaining within the cycle of birth and death, [is not lost].
Those who do not destroy their roots of goodness are not ungrateful;
those who destroy their roots of goodness are ungrateful.

For this reason, all Buddhas praise those who recognize and repay their debts of gratitude. Some ask: when the followers of Śākyamuni compose prefaces for laypeople, they also say, "Dedicated to the four debts of gratitude."
One might ask: who were his king, parents, teachers, and donors?
The answer is that the sutra does not say.
And those who have previously rendered benefit to the world,
upon whom others rely for their kindness—
whether through instruction in scriptures, arts, crafts, or occupations.
Those who cause others to avoid evil and follow the good are all teachers.
Now, a "teacher" (shi) is a designation for one who instructs others in the Way (Dao).
If one lends capital to relieve suffering and bestow happiness, such a person is also a donor.
Now, there are three kinds of giving:
first, the gift of wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), which refers to giving material goods to others.
The second is the gift of mind, which refers to bestowing happiness upon others through a heart of compassion and loving-kindness.
The third is the gift of Dharma, which refers to teaching the Dharma to benefit others and so forth.

Regarding filial piety (*xiào*), the *Erya* states: "To serve one's parents well is called filial piety. The *Shifa* (Methods of Posthumous Titles) states: "To love with compassion and forget one's own weariness is called filial piety. The *Zaji* (Miscellaneous Records) states: [as cited above].
To nurture virtue and accord with principle, not opposing the times, is called filial piety. The *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra* states:
The Buddha addressed his disciples:
Be cautious of your mental thoughts;
do not succumb to the five desires.
Rinse the passions and remove defilements.
Non-seeking is foremost;
internally one should be pure, and externally one should exhaustively practice filial piety. The Brahmajāla Sūtra says:

When the Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained supreme enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, establishing the dharma of filial piety toward one’s parents, teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels; for filial piety is the way to reach the Supreme Path, and thus filial piety is named "precepts. The *Ullambana Sūtra* states that the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to prepare offerings of food bowls for their parents of seven generations and to provide for the Buddha and the Saṃgha during the period of self-indulgence (*pravāraṇā*). While worldly people practice filial piety only for themselves, those of the Śākya lineage practice filial piety on behalf of their parents of seven generations; this may truly be called filial piety. The *Fayuan Zhulin* (Grove of Pearls from the Garden of Dharma) states that upholding the precepts is itself the practice of filial piety. This is because all sentient beings have once been one's own parents or kinsmen; therefore, now upholding the precepts by not killing, not stealing, and so forth, is what is called practicing filial piety.
The realms of existence (*dhātu-gati-dhātu*).
This refers to the three realms and the [five] destinies (*gati*).
That is to say, the six destinies. Master Yu’s preface states:
"Now, the three realms are established in their respective positions, and the six paths are divided into distinct categories."
The coarse and the subtle differ in appearance;
suffering and pleasure diverge in their traces.
When one contemplates their source and origin, [they are found to be one].
Not departing from form and mind,
when one examines their ultimate convergence,
they are nothing other than arising and ceasing.
Arising and ceasing within the cycle of saṃsāra—
this is called impermanence.
Form and mind are like shadows and illusions.
This is the root of suffering;
therefore, Nirvana is likened to a great river, while the Lotus Sūtra is compared to a burning house. The sages transcend and awaken to this truth.
Ceasing the carriage to return to the source and extricating oneself from the three realms,
one may thereafter cultivate the Way.
What is the meaning of the "three realms" (*dhātu*)?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
it has the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*).
The meaning of cause and the meaning of abiding and maintaining.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Regarding the meaning of "segment" (*skandha*):
the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Phonology) states it has the sense of "proceeding," while the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: [it has the sense of] "accumulation."
Regarding the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*):
because cause and effect are distinct,
there are three types.
There are four kinds of desire within the desire realm:
first, sentient beings;
second, forms.
The three types of nutriment;
fourth, sexual desire.
Their meaning is defined by rarity and necessity.
This realm is called the "Desire Realm" (kāmadhātu) because it is fully endowed with the four types of desire.
Within it, there are six heavens.
That is to say:
the Four Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Yāma, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati.
Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because there are forms that can be discerned and designated, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*)."
There are eighteen heavens.
That is to say, there are three heavens in the first dhyāna: the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
The Brahmā-purohita and Mahābrahmā;
these are the three heavens of the second dhyāna.
Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha,
and Ābhāsvara.
The third dhyāna has three heavens:
Parīttasubha (Limited Purity), Apramāṇaśubha (Immeasurable Purity), and [Śubhakṛtsna].
The Śubhakṛtsna [heaven].
There are nine heavens in the fourth dhyāna, including the Puṇyaprasava [heaven].
The Heaven of Merit-Love,
the Heaven of Vast Results,
and the Heaven of Non-Perception.
Avṛha. Atapa. Sudṛśa.
"Good Vision" (Sudarśana) and "Ultimate Form" (Akaniṣṭha).
Regarding the formless realm, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Because there is no form that can be discerned or designated, it is called "formless.
There are four heavens, namely:
the sphere of infinite space.
The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness,
and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vibhāṣā).
Question:
For what reason did the Blessed One establish the designation "abodes" (āyatana) for the four formless states?
Answer: It is in order to refute the heterodox views that hold the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) to be nirvāṇa without body,
the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) to be nirvāṇa of the boundless mind,
and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) to be the nirvāṇa of the pure accumulation.
Adhering to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the worldly, empty stūpa of nirvāṇa;
the Buddha taught that it is a place of birth.
Because it is not true liberation.
The ninth stage, the Stage of Mixed Dwelling in the Five Destinies, subsumes the three evil paths of the desire realm and the four continents.

The sixth stage, the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation, subsumes the first dhyāna’s three heavens. The seventh stage, the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Concentration, subsumes the second dhyāna.
The three heavens are subsumed under the fourth stage of the sublime bliss of detachment;
the five heavens are subsumed under the fifth stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; and the nine heavens are subsumed under the sixth stage of the sphere of infinite space.
The stage of the seven bases of consciousness;
the stage of the sphere of nothingness;
and the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The term "ground" (bhūmi) has four meanings:
abode, inclusion, cultivation, and pacification.
As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
1. Existence in the desire realm (kāmadhātu-bhava).
2. Existence in the form realm (rūpadhātu-bhava).
3. Existence in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-bhava).
What is the meaning of "existent"?
It refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
The Buddha said: "If karma can cause the continuity of future births, it is 'existence' (*bhava*); furthermore, because it arises and ceases, it is called 'existence.
That which falls within the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*) is 'existence.
Regarding the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), the Abhidharma states:"
The desire realm consists of fourteen [realms]:
namely, the four evil destinies and the four continents.
There are six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are seven in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
namely the heavens of the four dhyānas.
Furthermore, within the first dhyāna, one takes the Great Brahmā Heaven;
within the fourth dhyāna, one takes the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Including the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva),
there are four [realms] in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu),
namely the four stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
The *Fayuan wen* asks:
"It is not yet known for what reason the Great Brahma Heaven (*Mahābrahmā*) is separately established as existing within the First Dhyāna."
Answer: It refers to those non-Buddhist practitioners who maintain the view of permanence,
who reckon that the Great Brahmā Deva King is the sovereign capable of producing all things.
To go against it is to undergo birth and death;
to accord with it is to attain liberation.
Furthermore, the Great Brahma Heaven King also reckoned himself to be the sovereign creator of all things.
This permanence is true liberation.
It is only to shatter such emotional views that the Tathāgata establishes it as "one existence."
Furthermore, as for the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva),
the beings in that heaven receive a retribution of five hundred kalpas of fixed lifespan in a state of mindlessness;
non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon this to be true nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata, in order to refute that view and reveal that it is not true nirvāṇa,
separately established it as one of the "existents" (bhava).
Furthermore, he included the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens [among them].
This refers to Maheśvara, the Lord of Devas;
those non-Buddhists reckon him to be the creator and sovereign lord,
and they maintain that by taking refuge in him, one attains true liberation.
In order to refute that view,
it is separately established as a single existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, regarding the human realm, each of the four continents is established as a separate existence.
This means that because the suffering in the four realms of miserable rebirth is so great, sentient beings do not take pleasure in or become attached to them;
therefore, existence (*bhava*) is established separately.
In contrast, the human realm is superior to those, and sentient beings therein are deeply and intensely attached to it.
Because the retributions experienced in the four continents differ, each is established as a separate existence (*bhava*).
The trichiliocosm is the realm transformed by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Regarding the meaning of "world" (*loka*): the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
The world (*loka*) refers to the flow of transition;
the realm (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.
Furthermore, it is said:
The four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—along with the four intermediate directions and above and below, are called "realms" (dhātu).
The past, future, and present are called "time" (adhvan).
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
There are two worlds: first,
the world of sentient beings,
which refers to all sentient beings.
Second, the world of moving beings (*sattvāvāsa*).
As stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, and other texts:
it is the center of the four continents.
Mount Sumeru— its name in the pure Brahma-language being *Sumeru*—
is called "Wondrous High.
This mountain is surrounded on the outside by eight mountains.
There is the Great Iron Ring Mountain (Mahācakravāḍa) which encircles [the world] on all sides;
together with one sun and one moon, they revolve day and night, illuminating the four continents.
One such land is called a single *kṣetra*.
A collection of one thousand such lands is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍika lokadhātu*).
The accumulation of one thousand small world-systems is called a medium chiliocosm;
the accumulation of one thousand medium chiliocosms [is called a great trichiliocosm].
It is called a "great trichiliocosm" because it consists of three sets of thousands; thus,
it is named the "trichiliocosm of three thousand worlds."
"Gatis" refers to the five destinies:
first, the celestial realm; second, the human realm.
1. The three hells; 2. animals;
3. hungry ghosts.
This means that because the asuras are included within all four destinies,
they are now opened up as a separate destiny;
thus, it is called the "six destinies."
What is the meaning of "destiny" (*gati*)?
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
it means that which is gone toward.
These sentient beings go to the places where they are to take rebirth; therefore, they are called "destinies" (*gati*). The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The meaning of 'destiny' is that of going or arriving."
This means that the causes of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas enable sentient beings to reach their respective places of birth;
furthermore, because they signify the "paths," they are called the "six realms" (*ṣadgati*).
The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because they are the most excellent among all realms of existence and because they radiate brilliant light, they are called 'devas' (heavenly beings). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are four kinds of devas.
First, those born as devas,
which refers to those above the Four Heavenly Kings.
Second, those named devas, which refers to the current kings who are called "sons of heaven" (devaputra).
Third, the pure gods by birth,
namely the various noble ones born among human beings.
Fourth, the pure gods by rebirth.
These are the various noble ones born in the higher realms.
Regarding the causes for birth in the heavens, the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"One who fully cultivates the ten superior wholesome actions [is reborn there]."
One may be born among the gods of the scattered stage (vīkṣiptabhūmi) in the desire realm;
this occurs if one cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action that are associated with meditative concentration (samādhi).
Born in the heavens of the Form Realm,
if one practices the cultivation of detachment from form,
one remains far removed from body and speech.
Through association with meditative concentration, one is born in the formless realm. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"By virtue of upholding the precepts..."
Do not kill.
Do not steal.
Do not engage in sexual misconduct.
By means of these three virtues,
one attains rebirth in heaven. The *Bianyi Zhangrezizi Jing* (Sutra of the Householder’s Son Bianyi) states that there are five matters [for this].
One will attain rebirth in heaven by refraining from killing living beings and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Second, the virtuous and worthy do not steal;
they practice giving without greed and provide relief to all who are destitute.
Third is purity:
not violating the sexual conduct of outsiders, whether male or female;
guarding the precepts, observing the fasts, and practicing with diligence.
Fourth, to be sincere and truthful without deceiving others,
and to guard against the four faults of speech.
Fifth, not to drink alcohol.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that "human realm" (*manuṣya*) is called *manuṣya* in Sanskrit,
so named because they are able to employ mental volition (*manasikāra*).
By observing the tasks to be performed,
one may become either greatly conceited or able to attain tranquility.
Because the mind is tranquil, one is called a "human" (manuṣya). The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"For what reason is the human realm called *manuṣya*?
There are eight meanings for this."
First, intelligence;
second, superiority;
third, subtlety of mind.
Fourth, perfect enlightenment;
fifth, the preeminence of wisdom;
sixth, the ability to distinguish between the false and the true.
The seven factors of the noble path are the true vessel;
for the eight [factors] are governed by the karma of the intelligent.
As stated in the *Pudgala-karmavipāka-viśeṣa-sūtra*:
Due to having previously performed superior,
though inferior-grade, sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind,
one is born into the human realm. As the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of Intent) states:
There are five matters by which one may be born among humans and attain human nobility and honor.
First, the merit of giving is vast and far-reaching;
second, paying reverence to the Triple Gem and to elders;
third, practicing patience and remaining free from anger.
Fourth, being gentle and humble;
fifth, extensive learning in the sūtras and precepts.
Furthermore, there are five other matters.
First, practicing generosity toward the poor;
second, maintaining the precepts by refraining from the ten non-virtuous actions;
third, exercising patience without becoming agitated.
Fourth is encouraging others through diligence;
fifth is serving with single-minded devotion and loyalty.
These five matters lead to birth among human beings.
They shall possess great wealth and long life;
they shall be handsome and majestic,
and be revered by others.
There are five things that lead to birth among the lowly and base among human beings:
first, arrogance;
second, [disrespect] toward one's two parents.

and protecting the Buddha-dharma.
If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas,
his merit and wisdom will increase day by day.
Regarding the six ways of harmonious respect, Zhao Yun said:
"One initiates physical action with a compassionate mind;
