With a mind of loving-kindness, one initiates mental action;
if one receives abundant sustenance,
one shares it with others.
Maintaining pure ethical discipline and cultivating the wisdom that exhausts the outflows—
if one practices these six dharmas.
Then the multitude will be harmonious and submissive,
and there will be no discord or contention.
As the *Sūtra of Good Words and Dharma Verses* says:
Uttering harsh words, reviling others, and acting with arrogance and contempt toward them—
by giving rise to such conduct,
jealousy and resentment are born.
Using humble speech and compliant words,
one shows respect to others;
casting off resentment, one endures evil.
Envy and resentment will naturally perish.
Therefore, one who speaks must ensure that they themselves remain free from affliction.
Nor does one blame the multitude;
this is what it means to be able to speak well.
Regarding this, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "In the midst of the multitude, [one should avoid] evil retribution."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Maudgalyāyana saw a large-bodied being,
an elephant-like bhikṣu.
They wear garments of iron leaves;
their entire bodies are ablaze with fire;
they eat by placing hot iron balls in iron bowls.
He then questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"This sentient being, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha..."
Having become a bhikṣu,
he delighted in inciting disputes and litigation, causing dissension among the Saṃgha and engaging in various forms of verbal contention to prevent them from being in harmony.
Those who were previously residing there will loathe it and depart;
those yet to come will not arrive due to this causal condition of sin.
Having already entered hell, one undergoes immeasurable suffering;
for remaining offenses, one now receives this body with its nine apertures. Those of lofty knowledge among the multitude may take this as a warning.
Regarding the selection of friends— selection of friends, selection of friends, selection of friends— the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"If a person associates with wise and virtuous friends, they can cause both body and mind to be purified internally and externally."
This is what is called a truly good man. The *Vinaya* states:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "A virtuous friend..."
This is half of the holy life.
All practitioners,
through the power of a virtuous friend, [attain it].
Only then can it be accomplished.
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes the entirety of the holy life."
If one obtains a virtuous companion with whom to dwell,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished until even Nirvana; therefore,

The *Four Kinds of Friends* (*Catuḥsuhṛd-sūtra*) states: "Bai" (Pai) was the name of the Buddha when he was the teacher of King Lan-da during his causal stage. Bai said to the king:
"There are four kinds of friends."
It is just like a flower-friend:
when it is in bloom, one places it upon the head;
when it withers, one casts it away upon the ground.
To attach oneself when seeing wealth and status,
and to abandon one when they fall into poverty,
is precisely this [fault].
The second is like a scale-pan friend;
that is to say,
when an object is heavy, the head [of the scale] sinks low.
When objects are light, they tilt upward;
when there is something to be shared, one shows respect;
when there is nothing to be shared, one becomes arrogant.
It is so. The three are like mountain friends;
they are, for example, like a mountain of gold.
Birds and beasts flock to it;
their feathers and fur are bathed in its radiance.
Its nobility lies in its ability to bring glory to others.
To share in wealth and joy together— this is it.
Fourth, being like a friend to the earth.
The hundred grains and all material wealth depend upon it;
it bestows, provides, and protects them.
"To receive great kindness without acknowledging the virtue [of the benefactor]" refers to this.

Regarding the three essentials of friendship, the *Hetupratyaya-sūtra* (Causality Sūtra) states:
The brahmin Udāyin was intelligent and possessed great wisdom;

He said to the Prince,
"A friend has three essential duties:
first, whenever one sees a fault, they should immediately offer admonition and counsel."
Second, seeing others do good, one deeply gives rise to sympathetic joy.
Third, when others are in distress or hardship, one does not abandon them.
One who has obtained a virtuous friend constantly practices these four dharmas.
The *Nāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
First, one should be without pride or flattery and always maintain a respectful attitude;
second, one should be gentle and prudent in speech.
Third, not being conceited;
fourth, constantly receiving verbal instruction.
Regarding these seven dharmas of a kinsman and friend, the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states:
One becomes a true friend by possessing seven qualities:
first, being able to do what is difficult to do;
second, being able to give what is difficult to give.
Third, being able to endure what is difficult to endure;
fourth, communicating secret matters to one another;
fifth, mutually concealing [one's faults].
Sixth, not abandoning others when they encounter suffering.
Seventh, not treating the poor with contempt.
Regarding the five matters for viewing friends, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-sūtra* states:
1. Upon seeing someone commit an evil act, one should go to a secluded place to admonish and rebuke them so as to stop it.
2. Whenever there is an urgent matter, one should hasten to provide assistance and protection.
3. Regarding all private conversations [one should remain discreet].
4. One must not speak [of their faults] to others. 5.
One should always treat them with respect and deference. 6.
Whatever good things one possesses, one should share them with them in proportion to one's means.
The *Yōng rén yīn yì* states:
This refers to those who are habitually ignorant and deficient;
their minds lack restraint and caution.
Incapable of speaking the Dharma with their mouths and taking evil people as friends—
these are called commoners.
The *Ranxi Fobenxing Jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds of Cultivation) states:
The World-Honored One and the bhikṣu Nanda went to a fish market.
The Buddha instructed Nanda to take some grass for the fish.
After holding it for a short while, he discarded it.
When his hands were made to smell,
Nanda was asked about it and said:
There was only a foul, putrid odor.
Furthermore, he went to a perfumery and had some wrapping paper for incense brought;
after scooping up a small amount, he threw it away.
He questioned Nanda again,
and Nanda replied that he could only smell a fragrance.
The Buddha said to Nanda:
The mutual influence of virtuous friends and evil friends is likewise so.
If one associates with virtuous friends,
one will certainly attain widespread renown.
"Examine the spy" (the character *jiàn* is pronounced with the fourth tone).
This refers to being enticed by intermediary words and causing discord. The *Mūla-vinaya* states:
"Friends must not abandon one another merely because of the words of others."
If you hear the words of others, you should examine them well; that is, you should scrutinize their phrasing to discern whether they contain faults.

Regarding the *Dazhong fengding zhuzhu chanzhu* (The Chan Master Who Upholds the Dharma), who respectfully observed the *Song Dynasty Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* bestowed by the Sacred Court, it says:
The Regulations for the Abbot of the Chan Gate were first established by Master Daizhi Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou.
It states briefly:
Since the time of Shaoshi until Caoxi, the Chan school has largely resided in Vinaya monasteries;
although they occupied separate quarters,
they nonetheless engaged in the preaching of the Dharma and the maintenance of the community.
Lacking any established standard,
I have always harbored this concern;
I shall now provide a broad yet concise synthesis to resolve the matter.
Having established formal regulations,
he focused on ritual propriety; subsequently,
he conceived an innovative plan to establish a separate meditation retreat.
Anyone who possesses the eye of the Way and the virtues worthy of veneration is appointed as an Elder (sthavira).
Having become the master of transformation,
[he presides over the community].
He immediately took up residence in the abbot’s quarters,
which were like the chamber of Vimalakīrti,
rather than being used for private sleep.
In this monastery, no Buddha Hall is established;
only a Dharma Hall is built,
signifying that what the Buddhas and patriarchs have entrusted to us is held as most venerable in the present age.
The assembly of students gathered there,
whether few or many, high or low,
all entered among the Sangha.
Arrangements were made according to seniority in years since ordination;
long continuous beds were provided,
along with clothing racks.
Regarding the requisites for lodging:
when lying down, one must always rest the head at an angle against the edge of the bed,
with the right side facing downward in the auspicious posture.
As for sleeping, because he has already sat in meditation for a long time,
he merely reclines briefly; thus,
he maintains all four modes of deportment.
As for those who enter the room to request instruction,
they are left to their own diligence or indolence;
so it is with the entire assembly of the monastery.
Gathering at dawn and assembling at dusk,
the elders ascend the hall,
while the administrators and the assembly attend.
The wild geese stood to one side and listened intently as the guest and host exchanged questions and answers,
which served to clarify and exalt the essential tenets of the school.
The outer hall is established according to the Dharma.
Meals at both times— breakfast and lunch— are provided equally and universally,
with a commitment to frugality.
This signifies the simultaneous practice of both the formal rite and the food offering.
It is the performance of the *fushō-hō* (universal labor rite),
wherein strength is exerted equally by those above and below.
Ten administrative duties were established,
which were called the "Liaoshe" (Office Quarters).
Each Liaoshe was assigned one head official.
This was intended to ensure that each official attended to their respective duties.
However, there were those who assumed false names and wore stolen robes,
mingling among the pure assembly.
Furthermore, regarding matters that cause separate disturbances and commotion:
the Hall Venerable (Dang Weina) shall immediately inspect and remove those from their respective positions—
whether they be newly registered monks (guada dan) or those expelled from the monastery (bin chu-yuan).
I wish the noble assembly of pure monks well.
Should anyone among them commit a grave offense, they shall be struck with a staff;
their robes, alms bowl, and ritual implements shall be burned before the assembly.
They were sent out through a side gate to demonstrate their disgrace.
Examine this regulation in detail.
There are four benefits. First,
one does not defile the pure assembly,
because it engenders respectful faith.
Second, they do not violate the monastic form because they follow the Buddha’s regulations;
third, they do not disturb the public offices because they reduce litigation and lawsuits.
Fourth, not leaking [secrets] to the outside, for the purpose of protecting the fundamental tenets of the school.
Regarding the four officers in charge of affairs, the *Huiyao* (Essentials of the Monastery) states: [The first is] the *Jiansi* (Chief Administrator).
"Supervisor" (kanja) is a general title;
this is why it is not referred to as "abbot of the temple" (jiinshu).
This is a respectful designation for the two *karmadāna* (administrative officers), the second of whom is called the *rātrī-karmadāna*.
In Chinese, this is translated as "Joy-Maker" (*yuèzhòng*). The *Vinaya* states:
The Administrative Officer ○ III. The Seat Manager (*bhojanādhyakṣa*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The seat manager successively assigns the beds and seats."
This is one of the nine matters concerning the management of the Sangha. ○ Fourth, the *zhísuì* (Director of Affairs).

According to the *Sānqiānwéiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners), one who possesses ten virtues is qualified to serve as *zhísuì*; as the text is extensive, it is not recorded here in full.
Now, those who merely manage the monastery grounds and the seasonal laborers are appointed from among the four ranks above;
none of them are to be selected from the local disciples,
but must all be chosen from within the ocean-like assembly of monks from the ten directions.
He selected those whose minds were established in the Way, whose physical constitutions were robust, and who understood cause and effect.
He struck the wooden mallet and said,
"The assembly requests [the Dharma]."
If the person appointed to perform the service becomes weary of mind or body,
he shall announce this to the assembly and return to the hall;
another capable person shall then be specially invited to take his place.
The *Dharmatrāta-śāstra* (Chanzhidu lun) states:
"In the language of Qin, it means 'cultivation through contemplation' (*cintā-bhāvanā*). The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"It is called dhyāna because it severs the fetters. The *Preface to the Essentials of Dhyāna* states:
Without dhyāna there is no wisdom;
without wisdom there is no dhyāna.
Thus, dhyāna does not illuminate without wisdom.
Illumination cannot be achieved without dhyāna.
How great! Should one not diligently apply oneself to the practice of dhyāna and wisdom? The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Dhyāna..."
This is called "Universal Wisdom" (Puzhi).
It means that one can attain the Way and is also able to abandon the fetters.
This is the function of dhyāna.
If there is the name of dhyāna but no function of dhyāna,
it is termed "mud."
The Preface to the *Sūtra on the Expedient Means for the Practice of Dhyāna* by the Great Master Huiyuan of the Liang Dynasty states: "Now,
as for the arising of the three karmas..."
Taking dhyāna and prajñā as its fundamental principle,
although the refined and the coarse differ in their respective divisions,
there is a systematic method for ascending through them.
Therefore, as they set out upon their paths at the crossroads,
there was no confusion of tracks along the way.
When customs are transformed and affairs are established, merit does not depend on accumulation.
When one returns to stillness through its source,
then the subtle threads of the profound are made manifest.
It is profound and vast, difficult to exhaustively investigate.
Nevertheless, its principles are not obscure, and its essential purport may be understood; let me speak briefly.
Meditation is not wisdom.
Without it, one cannot exhaustively fathom its stillness;
without wisdom, there is no means to deepen the illumination of dhyāna.
Thus, these are the essentials of dhyāna and wisdom.
This is what is meant by "illumination within stillness.
Their characteristics are mutually supportive;
illumination does not depart from stillness.

Quiescence does not depart from illumination. When there is resonance, they move together; when there is response, they necessarily share the same destination. Their function is profound in its interpenetration, nourishing the myriad phenomena; this is the comprehensive essence of their subtlety.

They direct the multitude of movements toward the One without being anything in particular, and they expand the Great Image within the formless without being non-existent. They are without thought and without action, yet there is nothing they do not accomplish.
Therefore, those who wash their minds to still the turmoil employ it to investigate their thoughts and awaken to the subtle;
those who seek to exhaust the divine employ it to penetrate the profound.
(The *Sengshi lüe* states: [Note: The original Chinese text contains a section break marked by ○.]
"Chan" (Dhyāna) is a general term for meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā);
it is the path toward clarifying the mind and penetrating the principles of reality.
In the past, Bodhidharma observed that the spiritual capacities and conditions in this land had become disordered and chaotic during one particular period.
Thus it is said that "not relying on words and letters" is intended to dispel attachment to texts and stagnation in forms.
"Directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha" means...
This clarifies that [the teaching] is realized instantaneously as non-arising.
Because its capacity is steep and its principle profound,
those who practice through gradual cultivation earnestly slander it.
The *Record of the Mirror of Practice and Realization of Zen Monks* states:
There are ten aspects of the practice and realization of Zen monks.
First, clearly perceiving one's nature.
Just as one perceives forms during the day,
when encountering conditions and facing objects—
seeing forms, hearing sounds, lifting the feet, and setting them down.
Whether with eyes open or closed,
one attains clarity regarding the fundamental principle and enters into resonance with the Way.
Third, having surveyed the teachings of the lifetime of the Buddha and the words and phrases of the ancestral masters from antiquity,
one hears the profound without fear and attains clear understanding free from doubt.
Fourth, through various inquiries and challenges based on differences in causes, one is able to sever the doubts of others.
Fifth, at all times and in all places,
his wisdom shines forth without obstruction;
he perceives not a single dharma capable of acting as an impediment.
Sixth, one completely shatters consciousness regarding adverse and favorable conditions.
Seventh, when the mind and its objects arise, one understands their point of origin and is not deluded by the roots and dust of birth and death.
Eighth, within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—one reverently maintains mindfulness and attentiveness, ensuring that eating and drinking accord with the Way.
Ninth, whether hearing it said that there is a Buddha or no Buddha, or that sentient beings exist or do not exist,
one remains unmoved in single-mindedness whether they are praised or reviled.
Tenth, regarding the wisdom of differentiation.
They were all able to achieve clear penetration;
they mastered both nature and characteristics,
and were unimpeded in both principle and phenomena.
There is not a single dharma whose origin he does not discern.
The *Da zhuangyan lun* (Treatise on the Great Adornment), a distinct work of the Chan school, states:
"Such as these are the Saṃgha."
This is indeed the grove of supreme wisdom;
all movements of virtuous conduct gather therein.
Furthermore, in the Sanskrit language: [omitted].
Pindavana; this is translated as "Thicket" (Conglin), so named because the patriarch Śāṇavāsa resided there. It is located at Mount Shuangfeng under Caoxi in Shaoyou Prefecture.
Formerly, the residence of Sun Cao Shuliang, the Marquis of Wucheng of the Jin dynasty,
was converted into Bao Lin Temple,
where the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, resided. As the *Chansi Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Chan Quarter) states:

In the second year of the Tianbao era of the Qi dynasty, an imperial edict was issued for each province to establish separate quarters for Chan meditation. This was the site where the Western Indian Patriarch Śaṇakavāsin preached the Dharma at Qinglin. At Dongsi in Hunan, the Chan master Ruohui’s meditation cave had many halls and couches that had become sunken and broken from the weight of his numerous disciples.
At that time, it was again titled "Chan Cave. This is the site at Shaolin and Shaoshi where the Great Master Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years.
According to the *Naiyuan Neidian Lu*, the Kasmirian Chan Master Fashou stated: [text continues].
Upon first arriving in Dunhuang,
he immediately established a meditation hall and opened up a garden of one hundred mu.
A thousand *nai* trees were planted;
the assembly of practitioners gathered in great numbers,
arriving like clouds.
Regarding the *Sifen sengwu chao* (Excerpts on the Property of the Sangha of the Four Directions) concerning the maintenance of the Dharma in the ten directions, Master Shi explains:
"Four" encompasses the various quarters, while "ten" includes both ordinary beings and sages; this refers to all property belonging to a single monastic residence.
Although it is confined to a single realm,
its substance belongs to the Saṃgha of all ten directions;
as for those who arrive and reside therein:
There are no distinctions between ordinary people and sages, nor between kin and strangers;
those who come are not rejected, and those who depart face no obstacles.
The elders and administrators do not employ disciples from their own original monasteries.
I pray that you will select from among the ocean-like assembly in the ten directions those who possess the eye of the Way and virtuous conduct to serve as elders;
they shall reside in the main quarters and preach the Dharma at dawn and dusk to instruct the people.
If there are those with talent and capability who fear the law of cause and effect and have developed the aspiration for the Way, they are fit to serve as administrators;
the community should be assembled by sounding the *ghanṭī* to formally request their service.
When they eventually occupy these positions,
their virtue and conduct may lack substance,
and their talent and capability may be devoid of merit.
If one’s conduct is corrupt and evil,
one should also inform the assembly and withdraw with a bow.
When ordaining disciples, one should separately invite those who are capable.
There is only the Elder alone;
among the monks, there is no matter of individual differentiation.
Or, there may be monastic affairs that all perform together.
This means that each extends one hand;
since the benefits and offerings are distributed equally to all,
it is called "abiding and sustaining throughout the ten directions."
The Elder’s inspection of the quarters is now a regular custom in Chan monasteries.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"For five reasons, the World-Honored One would inspect the monks' cells once every five days."
First, the fear that disciples might become attached to conditioned phenomena;
second, the fear that they might become attached to worldly discourse;
third, the fear that they might become attached to sleep.
Fourth, for the purpose of tending to sick monks;
fifth, so that young bhikṣus may see the Buddha’s majestic deportment and likewise give rise to joy. Regarding the term *liáo* (chamber):

the *Táng yùn* states that those who share office are called *liáo*. Here, in the context of a Chan residence, the meaning is taken as many people living together and jointly attending to one task; thus it is called a *liáo*.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to distinguish the name of the dwelling for the *vinaya* (monastic discipline).
"Attendant" (*śrāmaṇera*) refers to those on the left and right of the Elder (*sthavira*).
Zhaò says:
Regarding those who serve with reverent self-possession and obedience to commands,
the *Sūtra on the Descent from Tuṣita* states that an attendant possesses eight qualities.
First, the faculty of faith is firm;
second, the mind seeks progress;
third, the body is free from illness.
Fourth, diligence;
fifth, possessing a mindful mind;
sixth, a mind free from arrogance.
Seventh, one is able to achieve concentration of mind.
Eighth, one is endowed with the wisdom of learning.
The *Samantapāsādikā* (The Universal Request Vinaya) states that this is because the Buddha spoke of the benefits of sweeping the ground.

At that time, the elder bhikṣus all abandoned their meditation and recitation to sweep the ground. The Buddha stopped them, saying, "I shall explain the duties of an administrator to those who serve as administrators.
Furthermore, because they did not sweep everywhere, the Buddha ordered the *ghanṭā* to be struck so that everyone would assemble together to perform the task.
This is the beginning of the *fushō* (general invitation).
The *Sōjishō* states:
"In the temple, monks are selected from the roster of the monastic community (*sōji*) and appointed as messengers to invite guests."

To reverse the names and skip their proper order would mean that this dwelling place cannot be called a "saṃgha," because it lacks the sense of harmony between host and guest. According to the Vinaya,
the maintenance of a community may involve those who share the same Dharma and the same food.
Alternatively, there are three officials who share the same dharma but have separate responsibilities for food and affairs;
these are called the "Three Pillars" (sāṅga). They are like the great ropes of a fishing net:

when pulled by them, the net becomes straight. First is the *Upādhyāya* (Sanskrit: *upādhyāya*), second is the *Vihārasvāmin* (Sanskrit: *vihārasvāmin*), and third is the *Karmadāna* (Sanskrit: *karmadāna*).
*Karmadāna* is translated here as "administrative officer.
*Poṣadha* is the standard procedure for the observance of the precepts according to this Vinaya.
This is called "dwelling together" (sāṃvāsika) or "pure dwelling" (śuddhavāsa). The *Vinaya* states:
*Poṣadha*—translated into Chinese as "nourishing purity" (*chángyǎng jìng*)—refers to removing the defilement of broken precepts in order to nourish and increase one's purity.

The intention is that every half-month one should recall the offenses committed and confess them before a person who has not themselves committed such an offense, thereby reforming previous transgressions;
first, this prevents further commission of them in the present.
Second, it is for the purpose of restraining future instances of contempt for the Dharma. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"What is called *poṣadha*? The answer is: 'cutting off' (*prati-saṃ-dhā*) is what is meant by *poṣadha*."
This means that it is able to sever what is to be done, sever the afflictions, and sever all unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Purity is called poṣadha."

*Śalākā*, the Sanskrit term for "counting sticks" (*cīhóu*), is translated here as "counting sticks. Regarding the origin of this Vinaya rule: once, a Brahmin asked the bhikṣus, "How many people currently reside in the Jeta Grove? The bhikṣus did not know. The Buddha said, "You should employ counting sticks."
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* on the Monk Who Manages Affairs states that the Buddha said:
"I permit two kinds of monks to manage affairs:
first, those who are able to maintain the precepts."
Second, regarding thoughts of future lives:
furthermore, there are those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) concerning the karmic retribution for their actions toward others.
For such people, managing communal affairs while remaining free from personal fault and protecting the intentions of others is difficult because of this.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states regarding "exerting force":
if a layperson intends to commit an evil act within the monastery to harass or disturb a bhikṣu,
one should sternly and forcefully subdue them.
Alternatively, one may speak directly to the king and his ministers to command them to cease their evil deeds.
Regarding the bhikṣu who guards the monastery, the *Śariputra-bhikṣu-vinaya* states:
"The Buddha sent a bhikṣu to guard the monastery during meal times; this is equivalent to the current practice of having a 'month-on-duty' bhikṣu in two monasteries to oversee the halls."

The *saṃgha-dūta* (monastic messenger) is generally dispatched from two temples to perform ritual duties and serve as a guest attendant; they ride with the letter and arrive first, and these are all *saṃgha-dūtas*.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who possesses eight qualities should be appointed."
First, the ability to listen;
second, the ability to speak;
third, self-understanding.
Fourth, causing others to understand;
fifth, being able to receive [the teaching];
sixth, being able to remember and uphold it.
Seventh, freedom from error;
eighth, the ability to distinguish between excellent and inferior speech and discourse. The verse says:
"When in the midst of a great assembly, his mind is free from timidity."
What he says does not add to what has been taught, nor does it diminish it;
his speech is free from confusion, and he does not waver when questioned—a bhikṣu such as this is fit to serve as a messenger for the Saṃgha.
The *Jōjūshō* states: "There are four kinds of monastic property (*sōmotsu*).

The first is 'permanent-permanent' (*jōjū-jōjū*), which refers to the dwellings, utensils, trees, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, rice, wheat, and other such items belonging to the community of monks (*saṃgha*). Because their substance is restricted to that specific location and does not extend to other boundaries, they may only be used and are not permitted to be divided or sold; thus, the term 'permanent' is stated twice."
The second is the permanent offering for the ten directions, such as the cooked food and other provisions offered to the Sangha within a single monastery.
While its substance extends throughout the ten directions, it is restricted solely to its original location.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
To eat without striking the bell constitutes the offense of theft. Nowadays, when food is fully prepared in various monasteries, the bells and drums are struck;

this is because they summon the Sangha from the ten directions, and thus these items belong to the ten directions. Third, regarding the *pratyutpanna* (present) and *sthāvara* (permanent/endowment) property, there are two types.

Furthermore, in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, when Wang Qiu died, Yan Yanzhi composed a funerary inscription for a stone monument that was erected; since then, the gentry families have followed this custom as a traditional practice. Moreover, Feng Jian’s *Xu Shishi* states:

According to the *Xijing zazhi* (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital), Du Zilin of the Former Han dynasty composed a text at the time of his death, ordering it to be carved on stone and buried before his tomb; it is likely that subsequent practices originated from this. The *Baiji liutie* (Six Categories of Bai Juyi) states: [as cited above].

At the funeral of Confucius, Gongxi Chi served as the *shi* (the marker); this refers to the funerary inscription. At the funeral of Zizhang, Gongming Yi served as the *shi*. This, moreover, did not originate in the Han or Wei periods. It is further stated that:

An inscription is a composition concerning the virtuous deeds of one's ancestors; when a gentleman observes such an inscription, he admires both what is praised therein and what the ancestor himself accomplished.
Therefore, the principle of an inscription is that it praises excellence and does not praise evil. To praise an ancestor who possesses no excellence is to commit a falsehood.
There are those who possess beauty but lack clarity;
there are those who possess knowledge but do not transmit it, which is unkind.

These three things are what the gentleman finds shameful. To summarize the essential points, I have omitted details and skipped over the sequence; however, the two masters among the sons of Śākya truly possess virtuous conduct and renowned achievements, and they too ought to be recognized.
This serves as the foundational basis for the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*).
Regarding the term "the orphan" (*gu*), the *Book of Rites* (*Quli*) states:
"The orphaned son presides over the household."
This refers to those whose age is not yet thirty.
When they reach their prime and establish a household,
they possess the basis for succeeding to the role of a parent.
"One does not call oneself 'orphaned' (gu).
Now I see that the Śākyaputrīyas refer to themselves as 'orphans.
Your disciples do not do so."
Goso Sōsan said:
"The term 'Kōin' (Loyalty Cloister) is appropriate for a junior disciple.
'Kō' refers to the mourning and loyalty observed during the period of bereavement."
If it is said by the laity that the "Hall of Filial Piety" (xiàotáng) is not a term used within our own tradition,
this applies to those who reside in the quarters of a large monastery.

"Light items belonging to the Saṃgha."

this was because the distribution had been uneven.

First, one should inform the assembly with words;
once they have harmoniously consented, it may be sold and divided. Regarding the five factors for speaking: [text continues].
Not following after craving,
not following after hatred,
and not following after delusion.
Not following after fear;
knowing gain and loss—this is also called the five virtues. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:
When a monk increases the price after a robe has been offered for sale but before the three calls have been completed,
and he later regrets it and suspects that he might be taking back the robe from the person who previously paid the price, the Buddha said:

Regarding the non-offense, the Mūlamadhyama-vinaya states:
The Buddha said,
"The first case is determined by the time [of the robe]."
One may set a middle price;
do not make it too expensive or too cheap.

If one does not purchase [the item] but intentionally increases the price, one commits an *dukkaṭa* offense. (From the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

In order to repay his profound virtue,

This is because the Śākya clan has no taboos regarding such matters.

they value avoiding meat, alcohol, and the intermingling of men and women.

Question: Regarding the presence or absence of consciousness within a grave, the *Kuan-ting ching* (Consecration Sutra) states:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "If a person's life has come to an end..."
[They] construct burial mounds and tombs.
Is the person's spirit and essence within them?
The Buddha said:
It is both existent and non-existent.
Why is this? Because if a person does not cultivate roots of goodness at the time of birth, [it is non-existent].
They do not recognize the Three Jewels;
they receive no merit for their good deeds,
nor do they suffer calamity for their evil ones.
Lacking virtuous friends to cultivate merit for him,
his spirit remains within the tomb.
Because there has been no place of birth [in this life],
or because they previously cultivated merit and goodness and practiced the Path with diligent effort.
Or they may be born among devas or humans;
therefore it is said that [the Buddha] is not present.
Or they may have previously lacked faith in the True and Right.
Deceitful, fraudulent, and deceptive toward others,
they commit evil karma and should fall into the realms of animals, malevolent ghosts, or hell.

There is no fault, for there is the authoritative word of the Noble One as proof. What is it? The *Buddha-mūla-prakṛti-carita-sūtra* (Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha) says:
There were some bhikṣus who,
having grasped the essential meaning and flavor from within the sūtras,
preached the Dharma to others without following the proper sequence.
They were apprehensive and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to act according to convenience."
From among the various sutras,
one selects the essential meanings and arranges them into prose and verse to preach the Dharma for others.
One should simply adopt the middle meaning;
do not distort the original sutra. The *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables* says:
"If there is an ordinary person who understands even a single phrase of a profound sutra..."
Reciting with the mouth and contemplating with the mind,
one [eliminates] the three poisons and four māras within the body,
as well as the eighty thousand gates of defilement.
If none of them can find peace for themselves,
how much less could one who extensively gathers various teachings serve as a bridge for the world?

Written with utmost reverence by the monk Xingmiao of the Xifa Hall. Postscript to the *Essentials of the Śākya Clan*, Volume Lower. Written at the time of his reinstatement as the Grand Master of the Central Dispersion (Zhong-san-dafu), serving as Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guangluqing) and Military Commander (Hujun) of Jiangning Prefecture, holding the Rank of Purple Golden Fish.

Master Cheng of Yue-lun Mountain in Qiantang, who had been granted the purple robe for his selection, cultivated lofty and pure conduct and mastered both internal and external learning. Untroubled by the affairs of the mundane world, he constantly found repose in mountain temples. Considering that the teachings of the Buddha were flourishing under the Sacred Dynasty and that the community of those clad in "field-garments" (monks) was vast, yet fearing that the sutras were so extensive that it would be difficult for students to master them all completely—lest the ignorance of beginners obscure the fundamental principles of renouncing the secular world—he examined the treasury of the *Ratnakūṭa* and thoroughly investigated the texts of the *Palm-leaf* scriptures. He categorized and synthesized their meanings, extracted the essential pivot points, and refined the contents; thus, the categories were fully established and the historical accounts were comprehensive and detailed. When one opens these words, they are as radiant as the melting of spring; when one examines their principles, they are as clear as ice dissolving. This work is truly like the *Xueji* of Confucian officials—it is the essential compendium of the Buddhist gate.

Cui Gong, Prefect of Piling Commandery and Director of the Bureau of Topography, possesses profound and vast knowledge and refined, exquisite talent; he has composed this *Ziyin* (Preface to Characters), the meaning and phrasing of which are most marvelous. Having had the good fortune to receive and read it, I am filled with boundless admiration. It is only fitting that it be carved upon wooden blocks to be transmitted so as not to perish. I have briefly compiled these notes, hoping to assist in its dissemination—thus I write. Recorded on the *xinhai* day of the final spring month in the Jiashizi year of the Tiancheng era.
